summary: Describes goals for integrating authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA) with Mobile IPv6 when it is offered as a service by a provider. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If a company lets your phone keep its address while roaming, it needs to know who you are, what you may do and what to bill you.

questions: how does aaa integrate with mobile ipv6
subtitle: Design goals for adding authentication, authorization and accounting to mobile IP services

tldr.problem: When a service provider offers Mobile IPv6 (the ability to keep your address while moving between networks), they need to verify who you are, what you're allowed to do, and track what to bill you for.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets design goals for integrating AAA infrastructure with Mobile IPv6 protocols through two interfaces: one between the AAA server and Home Agent for service authorization, and another between AAA and the network access point for configuration delivery.
tldr.outcome: These goals provide a framework for securing Mobile IPv6 deployments as a managed service, though actual implementation standards were specified separately.

today: RFC 5637 is an Informational document published in September 2009, describing goals rather than solutions. It has not been obsoleted, and these design goals provided the basis for later standards work on Mobile IPv6 and AAA integration, though the specification work happened separately in other documents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 lets a device keep its home address even when roaming between networks, enabling seamless mobility. But when companies offer this as a service, they face a challenge: the device, the home agent (which forwards traffic), and the network operator may all be different entities with different administrative domains. This document describes design goals for integrating Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) infrastructure with Mobile IPv6 to handle these scenarios.

The problem is known as the bootstrapping problem: how do mobile nodes get the configuration they need (like the home agent address and encryption keys) and how do all parties verify identity and permissions? AAA infrastructure, which already solves these problems for network access, can be reused here.
sections.plainLanguage: A moving phone needs to prove it's allowed to use a home agent, get the agent's address, set up secret keys, and let the company track its usage. AAA is the system that does this.

sections.title: Motivation and Bootstrapping
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 requires two key things to work: configuration parameters (a home address and home agent address) and cryptographic material (shared keys or certificates) to set up security. In two scenarios described in the RFC, the AAA infrastructure plays a central role. In the split scenario, the access service and mobility service come from different operators, so the home agent queries the home realm's AAA server to verify the user's Mobile IPv6 credentials and authorization. In the integrated scenario, the access and mobility services come from the same operator, and the AAA server provides the home agent information to the network access point during initial authentication.

Both scenarios require standardized message exchanges between the Home Agent and AAA server, and between the AAA server and the Network Access Server, to handle authentication and parameter delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two setups: one where your phone company and your mobility provider are different (split), and one where they're the same (integrated). In both cases, the AAA system needs to help deliver configuration and keys to the phone and the home agent.

sections.title: AAA-HA Interface Requirements
sections.content:
The document lists detailed design goals for the communication between the AAA server and the Home Agent. Key requirements include: reusing existing AAA security mechanisms for mutual authentication and integrity protection; allowing the AAA server to verify Mobile IPv6 service authorization using a Network Access Identifier (NAI); permitting the AAA server to send operational restrictions like packet filters and quality-of-service parameters; supporting authorization lifetime limits so sessions can expire; allowing the AAA server to force termination if credit is exhausted; and enabling different levels of Mobile IPv6 authorization (for example, standard Mobile IPv6 or Dual Stack Mobile IPv6 for IPv4 addresses).

The requirements also cover Mobile Node authentication, allowing the Home Agent to act as a pass-through EAP authenticator or to verify authentication credentials received from the mobile node, and the provisioning of configuration parameters such as the Home Address and the mobile node's fully qualified domain name for DNS updates.
sections.plainLanguage: The Home Agent and AAA server need to trust each other, check if the user is allowed to use the service, send authorization limits and restrictions, and share the configuration the phone needs.

sections.title: AAA-NAS Interface Requirements
sections.content: The integrated scenario also requires design goals for the AAA server's communication with the Network Access Server (the network access point). These goals are simpler: the AAA server must communicate the Home Agent information (IP address or fully qualified domain name) to the NAS; the NAS must signal whether it supports these extensions; the NAS must be able to suggest a home agent address in its domain if one is available; and the AAA server must indicate whether the mobile node is authorized to use a local home agent in the visited network or must use one from the home domain. Additionally, the solution must support cases where different AAA servers handle access authentication and mobility service authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: When the access and mobility services are the same, the AAA server tells the network access point what home agent to use, and the access point tells the AAA server if it can support that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC emphasizes that the AAA-HA interface must provide mutual authentication between the Home Agent and the AAA server, integrity protection for all exchanged data, and replay protection to prevent reuse of old messages. When security parameters such as IKEv2 pre-shared keys are transferred through this interface, confidentiality protection is strongly recommended. The document assumes a trust model where end users share credentials with their home AAA server and where communication links between AAA components may be protected. When the Home Agent and AAA server are in different administrative domains, roaming agreements between operators typically define the trust relationship.
sections.plainLanguage: The Home Agent and AAA server must trust and verify each other, check that messages haven't been changed or replayed, and protect secret keys when they're sent.
